title: Kafka: a distributed log
problem: A queue deletes each message once one worker acks it, so a second team cannot read the same events later and nothing can be replayed after a bug.
summary: Kafka is a partitioned, replicated, append-only log. Producers append to partition leaders, followers copy the records, consumers read by offset and keep their own position, and records stay for a retention period or are compacted down to the latest value per key.
catTip: I nap on the broker because it never throws anything away: every record stays, in order, until retention says otherwise. I keep my own bookmark, called an offset, and if I oversleep for a week the log has moved on without me.

recall.q: A producer sends with acks=all. What does it actually wait for, and why does min.insync.replicas still matter?
recall.a: The leader acknowledges only after every replica in the in-sync replica set (ISR) has the record. If the ISR has shrunk to the leader alone that is a single copy, so min.insync.replicas (typically 2 with replication factor 3) makes the broker refuse the write with NotEnoughReplicas instead of accepting it on one broker.

guide.breaks: A classic queue deletes each message once a consumer acks it, so a second consumer never sees the same events, nothing can be replayed after a bug, and ordering is lost on redelivery.
guide.tradeoffs: Keeping every record for days costs disk and moves the what-have-I-handled bookkeeping to each consumer, and strong durability (acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2) adds a wait for a second broker on every write.
guide.explainSimply: Kafka is a numbered ledger that is never erased: new entries go at the end, and each reader keeps a bookmark instead of tearing pages out. The ledger is copied to several machines so losing one loses nothing, and old volumes are shredded after a set time.
guide.hint: Think about who must hold the record before the leader says yes, and what 'everyone in sync' means when only the leader is in sync.

meow: Meow-ssages go in at the end, stay for seven days, and I read them by offset. Three copies, two must purr back before the write counts.

quiz.prompt: A topic has replication factor 3 and min.insync.replicas=2, and the producer uses acks=all. One broker is down, so a partition's ISR is the leader plus one follower. What happens to a produce request?
options: It fails with NotEnoughReplicas because one replica is missing
It succeeds once the leader and the remaining in-sync follower have both written it
It succeeds as soon as the leader has written it, because acks=all only waits for live followers
It blocks until the third replica comes back
quiz.explanation: acks=all waits for every current ISR member, here two brokers, which satisfies min.insync.replicas=2. It would fail only if the ISR shrank below two; the leader-only option describes acks=1, not acks=all.

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes a Kafka topic from a traditional message queue?
options: Kafka deletes a record as soon as a consumer acknowledges it
Kafka keeps records for a retention period regardless of consumption, so several consumer groups can read and replay the same records
Kafka guarantees ordering across all partitions of a topic
Kafka pushes records to consumers to keep latency low
quiz.explanation: Retention is by time or size, not by consumption, which is what makes replay and independent readers possible. Ordering holds only within a partition, and consumers pull rather than being pushed to.

cards.q: A follower broker's disk slows down and it stops keeping up. What happens to the partition's ISR, and to producers using acks=all?
cards.a: After replica.lag.time.max.ms (30 s by default) the leader drops it from the in-sync replica set. Writes keep being acknowledged by the remaining ISR members as long as the ISR still has at least min.insync.replicas brokers; below that, producers get NotEnoughReplicas.

cards.q: You keep every product's current price in a Kafka topic that must never lose the latest value but must not grow forever. Which retention policy do you use, and how do you delete a product?
cards.a: Log compaction (cleanup.policy=compact), which keeps at least the latest record per key and leaves offsets and ordering intact. Delete a product by writing a tombstone, its key with a null value, which compaction keeps for delete.retention.ms (1 day by default) so slow consumers still see the deletion.

glossary.note: The replicas of a partition that are caught up with the leader; a record is committed once all of them have it.
